items.followUp: What happens to the chromosomes during the S phase of the cell cycle?

rubric.why: Identifies the cell’s continued growth during G2.
rubric.description: The cell continues to grow during G2.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the cell grows or continues to grow.

rubric.why: Recognizes that G2 prepares the cell for mitosis, including by producing needed materials.
rubric.description: The cell prepares for mitosis by synthesizing proteins and other materials needed for division.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing preparation for mitosis or naming a needed material synthesized in G2.

modelAnswer: During G2, the cell continues to grow.
It synthesizes proteins and organelles and prepares for mitosis.

items.followUp: State two ways in which mitosis helps an organism.

rubric.why: Connects the increase in cell number to growth.
rubric.description: Mitosis increases cell number and enables growth.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that mitosis increases cell number for growth.

rubric.why: Identifies another role of mitosis in repair, replacement or development.
rubric.description: Mitosis repairs or replaces cells and contributes to development from the zygote.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing cell repair or replacement, or development from the zygote.

modelAnswer: Mitosis produces more cells, increasing cell number and enabling growth.
It replaces or repairs damaged and worn-out cells and helps in the development of an organism from the zygote.

items.followUp: At what stage of meiosis does crossing over occur, and what can it produce?

rubric.why: Checks the definition of crossing over and when it occurs.
rubric.description: Crossing over is the exchange of corresponding segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes during prophase I.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the exchange between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes in prophase I.

rubric.why: Checks that the diagram represents the original chromatids and the exchanged segments.
rubric.description: Diagram showing an exchange between two non-sister chromatids, with recombinant chromatids after the exchange.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a diagram showing the two original chromatids and the two recombinant chromatids.

modelAnswer: Crossing over is the exchange of corresponding segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes during prophase I of meiosis.
Before crossing over: chromatid 1 ABCD; chromatid 2 abcd.
After crossing over: chromatid 1 ABcd; chromatid 2 abCD.
The exchanged segments produce new combinations of genetic material.

items.followUp: Name the three main components of an ATP molecule.

rubric.why: Checks the components that make up ATP.
rubric.description: ATP consists of adenine, ribose sugar and three phosphate groups.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming all three components.

rubric.why: Checks that the structure shows adenosine linked to three phosphate groups.
rubric.description: A labeled structure showing adenine and ribose linked to three phosphate groups.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a structure showing adenine, ribose and the chain of three phosphate groups.

modelAnswer: ATP consists of adenine, ribose sugar and three phosphate groups.
The bonds between the phosphate groups are high-energy bonds.

items.followUp: What is the difference between a linear and a cyclic metabolic pathway?

rubric.why: Checks the basic meaning of a metabolic pathway.
rubric.description: A metabolic pathway is a series of chemical reactions that occur in a cell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining it as a series or sequence of reactions in a cell.

rubric.why: Checks how successive reactions in a pathway are controlled and linked.
rubric.description: Each reaction is enzyme-controlled, and the product of one reaction may become the substrate for the next.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the reactions are enzyme-controlled and linking a product to a subsequent substrate.

modelAnswer: A metabolic pathway is a series of chemical reactions that occur in a cell.
Each reaction is controlled by an enzyme, and the product of one reaction may become the substrate for the next reaction.

items.followUp: How does the shape of an enzyme’s active site help it catalyse a reaction?

rubric.why: Identifies the active site as the enzyme region where the substrate binds.
rubric.description: The active site is the specific region of an enzyme to which its substrate binds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying it as the specific enzyme region where the substrate binds.

rubric.why: Explains the relationship between the active-site shape and substrate binding.
rubric.description: The active site has a complementary shape to the substrate, allowing an enzyme-substrate complex to form.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining the complementary fit or formation of the enzyme-substrate complex.

modelAnswer: The active site is the specific region of an enzyme to which its substrate binds.
Its shape is complementary to the substrate, so an enzyme-substrate complex can form.

items.followUp: What happens to an enzyme’s activity when the temperature rises above its optimum temperature?

rubric.why: Describes the effect of increasing temperature up to the optimum.
rubric.description: The rate of enzyme action increases as temperature rises up to the enzyme’s optimum temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the rate increases up to an optimum temperature.

rubric.why: Explains why high temperatures reduce enzyme activity.
rubric.description: Above the optimum, denaturation changes the active site and decreases the rate of enzyme action.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking denaturation or a changed active site to a decrease in the rate.

modelAnswer: As temperature rises, the rate of enzyme action increases up to the enzyme’s optimum temperature.
Above the optimum, the enzyme may denature; its active site changes shape and the rate of enzyme action decreases.
